title: Tikhon of Zadonsk
hookLine: a bishop who gave away his bishop's comforts to live simply among the poor

lines: A BOW INSTEAD OF A BLOW.
A BISHOP WHO GAVE IT ALL UP.
cards: There's a story told about a Russian bishop and a quarrel. A proud nobleman, losing an argument with him, struck him across the face. The bishop didn't strike back, and didn't storm out.
Tradition says he bowed down to the floor in front of the man and asked his forgiveness for having provoked him. The nobleman, shaken, ended up on his knees too.
This bishop had already stepped away from what a bishop gets: the palace, the standing, the comforts.

teach.b: Tikhon was a Russian Orthodox bishop who served the diocese of Voronezh. He worked hard at it, opening schools and teaching his clergy, until his health broke down.
Then he asked to step aside, and went to live in a monastery at Zadonsk, near the river Don.
There he lived very simply, in a plain cell, and gave away what came to him, food, clothes, money, to the poor who lined up at his door. He visited prisoners. He sat with peasants.
People came to him for counsel, as they would to one of the elders we met yesterday.
His writings return again and again to one habit of mind: everything around you can point to God, even the plainest things you pass every day.
He wrote a book on just that, gathering spiritual lessons from ordinary things. It leads to our line: all is from God. Tikhon didn't mean that every cruelty is God's wish.
He meant that nothing, not even trouble, falls outside God's care, so a person can receive good days and bad ones with trust.
It echoes Paul's letter to the Romans: "all things work together for good to them that love God." It also sheds light on the bow after the slap.
If even an insult can be received from God's hand, then, as Tikhon saw it, there was no need to defend his dignity with his fists.
The Russian novelist Fyodor Dostoevsky admired him, and some readers see Tikhon behind the gentle elder Zosima in The Brothers Karamazov. The Orthodox Church honors him as a saint.

how: The Orthodox Church remembers Tikhon of Zadonsk as a saint with feast days in its calendar, and his writings on prayer and on seeing God in ordinary things are still read in Orthodox homes and monasteries.

practice: Let go of one small comfort you'd normally reach for right now, the cushion, the snack, the extra blanket, and sit without it, noticing what you feel.
If you pray, offer the small lack to God, or think of someone who goes without every day; if you don't, notice the gap, and think of who might use what you didn't.

wordCard.voice: Tikhon. The Russian bishop who stepped aside from a grand life, lived simply at Zadonsk, and taught that everything can point to God.

carryVoice: Your line: all is from God. That ends a week of preachers, poets and monks: Whitefield's born again, Edwards and the heart, Isaac Watts's hymn, Amazing grace, the Philokalia, Paisius, and Tikhon. A week, done.
